# Rule reference

All 34 rules Rescue Kit applies, grouped by category and ordered by severity.

This page is generated from the ruleset, so it always matches what the tool actually does.

## At a glance

| | Critical | High | Medium | Low | Total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Secrets & configuration** | 4 | — | — | 1 | 5 |
| **Authentication & access** | 4 | 2 | 1 | — | 7 |
| **Payments** | 2 | 1 | 1 | — | 4 |
| **Data & schema** | 2 | 2 | 1 | — | 5 |
| **Testing & CI** | — | 3 | 2 | 1 | 6 |
| **Operations & scaling** | — | 2 | 2 | 3 | 7 |
| **All** | 12 | 10 | 7 | 5 | **34** |

A project failing every applicable rule would carry an estimated 224 engineer-hours of remediation.

## What the severities mean

| Severity | Meaning | Score cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Critical** | Exploitable in production right now, or money/data already at risk | −50 to its category |
| **High** | No live exploit, but a serious gap that will cause incidents under real traffic | −22 |
| **Medium** | Will cause avoidable pain — duplicate charges, unreproducible builds, slow queries | −9 |
| **Low** | Worth fixing, costs little, blocks nothing | −3 |

See [the scoring model](./scoring.md) for how these combine into a grade.

## Secrets & configuration

Credentials that have escaped, or are one build away from escaping. These are weighted most heavily because they are the least recoverable: a key that reached a browser bundle or a git history is already public.

### `secrets/committed-env`

**Environment file is not excluded from version control**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| critical | 2h | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Add `.env*` to .gitignore (keeping `!.env.example`), then rotate every credential the file contains — git history keeps them recoverable even after deletion. Use `git filter-repo` to purge them from history if the repo is public.

### `secrets/hardcoded-credential`

**Credentials hardcoded in source**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| critical | 4h (~0.5d) | always |

**Fix:** Move each value to an environment variable read at runtime, rotate the exposed credential at the provider, and purge it from git history. Add a pre-commit secret scanner so this cannot recur.

### `secrets/public-env-secret`

**Secret exposed through a public environment variable**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| critical | 3h (~0.4d) | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Rename the variable to drop the public prefix and move every use of it to server-side code — an API route, server action, or backend service. Then rotate it: the current value is in the browser bundle and must be treated as public.

### `secrets/service-role-client-side`

**Privileged database key used outside server code**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| critical | 6h (~0.8d) | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Service-role keys bypass row-level security entirely. Use the anon/publishable key in client code and move every privileged operation behind a server route that checks the caller's identity first.

### `secrets/no-env-example`

**No .env.example documenting required configuration**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| low | 1h | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Commit a `.env.example` listing every variable the app reads, with placeholder values and a one-line comment each. It is the fastest onboarding win available and it prevents production outages caused by a missing variable.

## Authentication & access

Who the caller is, and what they are allowed to do. The most common source of exploitable bugs in prototype code, because auth is the part an app appears to work perfectly well without.

### `auth/plaintext-password-storage`

**Passwords handled without a hashing library**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| critical | 8h (~1d) | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Hash with argon2id or bcrypt before storage, and never log or return the field. If passwords have already been stored in plain text, force a reset for every account — the existing values cannot be made safe retroactively.

### `auth/trusts-client-supplied-role`

**Privilege decided by client-supplied data**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| critical | 8h (~1d) | always |

**Fix:** Read roles and permissions from the server-side session or from the database record for the authenticated user — never from the request body, query string, headers or local storage, all of which the caller controls.

### `auth/unprotected-route-handlers`

**API routes with no authorisation check**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| critical | 12h (~1.5d) | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Establish the caller's identity at the top of every handler and fail closed. Better still, enforce it centrally in middleware so a new route is protected by default rather than protected by whoever remembers — the default should be denial.

### `auth/weak-password-hashing`

**Passwords hashed with an unsuitable algorithm**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| critical | 6h (~0.8d) | always |

**Fix:** Replace with argon2id or bcrypt. MD5, SHA-1 and bare SHA-256 are fast by design, which is exactly wrong for passwords — a commodity GPU tries billions of candidates per second against them.

### `auth/jwt-decoded-without-verification`

**JWT decoded without verifying its signature**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| high | 4h (~0.5d) | always |

**Fix:** Use `jwt.verify` (or `jwtVerify` from jose) with the signing key. Decoding without verification is equivalent to trusting whatever the caller pasted in, because the payload is only base64 — anyone can forge one.

### `auth/no-authentication`

**No authentication mechanism detected**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| high | 16h (~2d) | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Adopt a maintained auth provider rather than hand-rolling sessions — Auth.js, Clerk, Supabase Auth and Better Auth all handle session rotation, CSRF and password reset correctly. Hand-written auth is where most prototype security bugs originate.

### `auth/no-central-route-protection`

**No middleware enforcing authentication centrally**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| medium | 4h (~0.5d) | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Add a `middleware.ts` matching your protected path prefixes so access control is applied by default. Per-route checks work until someone adds a route and forgets — and that failure is silent.

## Payments

Taking money correctly. These rules only run when a payment provider is installed. Every one of them corresponds to a way prototypes lose real money — to fraud, to duplicate charges, or to orders that are paid for and never fulfilled.

### `payments/client-supplied-amount`

**Charge amount taken from the client**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| critical | 8h (~1d) | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Send only a product or price identifier from the client, then look the real amount up server-side from your own database or the provider's price objects. The client may choose *what* to buy, never *what it costs*.

### `payments/unverified-webhook`

**Payment webhook accepts unverified requests**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| critical | 6h (~0.8d) | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Verify the signature header against the raw request body using the provider's SDK before trusting any part of the payload, and reject anything that fails. Note that the check needs the *raw* body — frameworks that parse JSON automatically will break verification silently.

### `payments/no-webhook-handler`

**No payment webhook handler**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| high | 10h (~1.3d) | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Fulfil orders from the webhook, not from the post-checkout redirect. Users close the tab, lose signal, and get redirected before the callback runs; asynchronous payment methods settle minutes later. Without a webhook those customers pay and receive nothing.

### `payments/no-idempotency-key`

**Payment writes without idempotency keys**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| medium | 4h (~0.5d) | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Pass an idempotency key derived from your own order identifier on every charge-creating call. Networks retry, users double-click, and webhooks are delivered more than once by design — without a key, each of those becomes a duplicate charge.

## Data & schema

The database and what reaches it. Covers both security (injection, row-level security) and the schema decisions that are invisible on seed data and painful at scale.

### `data/rls-not-configured`

**Row-level security not configured**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| critical | 16h (~2d) | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Enable RLS on every table holding user data and write policies covering select, insert, update and delete. Supabase exposes the database directly to the browser through PostgREST — without policies, the anon key is a full database client.

### `data/sql-string-interpolation`

**SQL built by string interpolation**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| critical | 8h (~1d) | always |

**Fix:** Use parameterised queries or the ORM's query builder. Prisma's `$queryRaw` tagged template and Drizzle's `sql` helper parameterise automatically — the danger is `$queryRawUnsafe` and manual string concatenation.

### `data/no-input-validation`

**Request bodies used without validation**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| high | 12h (~1.5d) | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Parse every request body through a schema at the boundary and reject what does not match. Beyond preventing malformed data reaching the database, it gives you correct types for free instead of assertions that lie.

### `data/no-migrations`

**No database migrations**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| high | 8h (~1d) | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Generate an initial migration from the current schema and commit it, then make migrations the only way schema changes reach an environment. Without them there is no repeatable way to stand up a new environment and no way to roll a bad change back.

### `data/unindexed-foreign-keys`

**Foreign keys without indexes**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| medium | 3h (~0.4d) | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Add `@@index([foreignKeyField])` for each relation scalar. Postgres does not index foreign keys automatically, so these become sequential scans — invisible on seed data, then suddenly the reason the app is slow at ten thousand rows.

## Testing & CI

Whether anything verifies a change before users do. Weighted lower than security categories — not because it matters less, but because it is recoverable: you can add tests next sprint with no lasting harm.

### `testing/build-ignores-errors`

**Build configured to ignore type and lint errors**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| high | 8h (~1d) | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Remove `ignoreBuildErrors` and `ignoreDuringBuilds`, then fix what surfaces. These flags are usually added to unblock one deploy and never removed, after which the type system stops providing any guarantee at all.

### `testing/no-ci`

**No continuous integration**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| high | 4h (~0.5d) | always |

**Fix:** Add a workflow running install, typecheck, lint and test on every push and pull request. Tests that only run when someone remembers are tests that stop passing without anyone noticing.

### `testing/no-tests`

**No automated tests**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| high | 24h (~3d) | always |

**Fix:** Start with the paths where a defect costs money — auth, checkout, anything writing to the database — rather than chasing a coverage percentage. A dozen tests on critical flows are worth more than a hundred on presentational components.

### `testing/no-test-script`

**No usable test command**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| medium | 2h | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Add a real `test` script to package.json. Contributors and CI both look there first, and a placeholder that exits non-zero means nobody can run the suite without reading the config.

### `testing/thin-coverage`

**Very few tests relative to the codebase**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| medium | 16h (~2d) | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Identify the flows a failure would actually hurt and cover those first. Add a regression test with every bug fix — that habit builds a suite shaped by real failures rather than by guesswork.

### `testing/no-typecheck-in-ci`

**CI does not typecheck**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| low | 1h | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Add `tsc --noEmit` as a CI step. Next.js and Vite builds skip type errors by default, so a type error can reach production without anything failing.

## Operations & scaling

Running the thing once it is live. Error visibility, abuse resistance, reproducible builds.

### `ops/no-error-tracking`

**No error tracking**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| high | 3h (~0.4d) | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Wire up Sentry or an equivalent on both server and client, with release tagging and source maps uploaded. Without it, production errors are only visible when a user takes the trouble to report one — and most will simply leave.

### `ops/no-rate-limiting`

**Public endpoints with no rate limiting**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| high | 6h (~0.8d) | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Rate limit by IP and by account on anything unauthenticated, and especially on endpoints that send email, reset passwords, or call a paid API. Without it, one script turns your endpoints into someone else's free resource and your bill into their problem.

### `ops/no-lockfile`

**No dependency lockfile**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| medium | 1h | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Commit the lockfile your package manager generates. Without one, two installs a week apart resolve different versions, which is how "works on my machine" becomes a production incident nobody can reproduce.

### `ops/no-security-headers`

**No security headers configured**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| medium | 4h (~0.5d) | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Set Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options and Referrer-Policy — in `next.config` headers for Next.js, or via helmet for Express. CSP is the meaningful one and takes the most tuning, so start it in report-only mode.

### `ops/debug-logging-left-in`

**Debug logging left in application code**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| low | 3h (~0.4d) | always |

**Fix:** Replace with a structured logger that has levels and can be turned down in production. Beyond the noise, console statements routinely log request bodies and tokens straight into whatever aggregates your output.

### `ops/no-node-version-pinned`

**Node version not pinned**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| low | 1h | conditional — see below |

**Fix:** Add an `engines.node` field and a `.nvmrc`. Hosting platforms otherwise pick a default that changes without warning, and the resulting failure appears at deploy time with no related code change to blame.

### `ops/no-readme`

**No README**

| Severity | Effort | Runs when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| low | 2h | always |

**Fix:** Document what the project is, how to run it locally, what configuration it needs, and how it deploys. Four short sections is enough, and it is the difference between a day and a week for whoever inherits this.

## Conditional rules

Rules marked *conditional* are skipped when they cannot apply — for example, payment rules on a project with no payment provider installed. A skipped rule does not count as a pass: **its whole category is excluded from the score** rather than credited. Crediting a project for security it does not implement would inflate every score and make comparison meaningless.

Run with `--json` to see `rulesRun` and `rulesSkipped` for a given project.

## Proposing a rule

Rules are small — a data object, a `run` function, and two tests. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md).
